column1: # suites.tsv - what each suite is, and which lanes run it.
# This had sixty-two rows for eighteen suites, because a row was one suite on
# one lane and five lanes ran nearly the same list. Twenty-nine of those rows
# were duplicates of another: `verify-std.sh doc` appeared five times, and the
# file could not say that the five were one thing.
# `lanes` is a space-separated list, or `*` for every lane, which is exactly how
# cases.tsv's `applies-to` already works. A suite that genuinely differs takes a
# second row with a disjoint lane list -- walk runs the release build on gjs and
# the testing build on kde, and that is a fact worth two rows. Disjoint and not
# ordered: which row applies to a lane is never a question of precedence, and
# selftest asserts no lane is claimed twice for one suite.
# `setup` is space-separated directives from the closed vocabulary in
# test/run.sh. An unknown directive is an error and not a shrug.
# `command` is argv, split on whitespace, run through test/lib/step.sh. It does
# not name the artifact: `build=` and `app=` do that, and run.sh appends the
# paths it just built. It also does not name the toolkit or the screenshot
# File order is run order, and with one list it is one order: each lane runs the
# subsequence of these rows that names it. It fits every lane as it was but one
# -- macos ran `walk` before `loaders` and the other four ran them the other way
# round, and no single sequence holds both. macos runs loaders first here.
# That is a smaller change than it reads as, and the reason is worth knowing
# before trusting this paragraph: CI does not run a lane, it runs a suite. Every
# lane is a column of `run.sh <lane> <suite>` steps in ci.yml, one per row, so
# the order a runner executes is the workflow's and this file's order never
# reaches it. What the sequence here governs is `bash test/run.sh macos` with no
# suite named -- a whole lane at once, which is a thing a person does on a desk
# Provisioning is not a suite. apt, brew, sysctl, setup-zig, docker login, the
# engine-removal guards, anything reading a secret and anything with a ${{ }} in
# it stays in the workflow, which is the thing that owns the machine. So do the
# The two Windows lanes have no rows: their steps are `shell: pwsh` and this
# column is argv for bash. Their builds do come from the tables --
# `run.sh --build <slot>=<build>` -- so what they run is declared even where how
# bsd, kde-live, wayland and macos-netinstall have no rows either, and that is
# not a migration left half-done: they run netinstall/test/run.sh or qtkde.sh.
